chunks: "Dropout voltage is mostly an LDO term: it's how much headroom the regulator needs between input and output before it falls out of regulation.
It's basically the output current times the on-resistance of the pass transistor, so it grows with load.

For an LDO, efficiency is just V out over V in , so more headroom is more heat, and close to dropout the pass device is wide open so you lose gain and the power-supply rejection collapses, which means ripple and noise from the input leak to the output.
A buck has a similar limit but it shows up as maximum duty cycle.
If V in drops toward V out , the duty has to go toward 100 percent, and the controller runs out of room because it needs a minimum off-time.
In that corner you get a dropout of roughly I out times the high-side resistance plus inductor DCR, and some parts just hold the switch on.
For a buck, higher V in means more ripple current and more switching loss, so efficiency drops and ripple grows.
Higher V out at the same input usually improves efficiency because the same loss is spread over more power.
And output current gives the familiar curve: bad at light load from fixed losses, best in the middle, and falling at the top from I to the 2R ."
